column4: The source section’s root ص ل ي links entering fire with ritual prayer; this ayah uses that same root for the blaze awaiting those who consume orphans’ property.
This ayah says those who commit aggression will be made to enter a fire, using the source section’s root ص ل ي in its fire-entry sense.
The rejected signs lead to a fire that repeatedly burns and replaces their skins; the fire-entry verb belongs to the source section’s ص ل ي root.
The source section links turning away with fire and failed worship; this ayah pairs turning away from the Messenger with being made to enter Hell, using the same fire-entry root ص ل ي.
Those who exchange gratitude for disbelief settle their people in ruin, Hell, where they burn; the fire-entry verb is the source section’s root ص ل ي.
This ayah identifies who is most deserving of burning in Hell, using the same ص ل ي root that the source section hears in 88:4.
The condemned are told to enter the Fire that day for their disbelief; the command uses the source section’s ص ل ي fire-entry root.
The ayah excludes from misguidance those destined to burn in Hell, using the source section’s ص ل ي root for entering the fire.
In the exchange between Hell’s groups, this ayah says the new arrivals will burn in the Fire, using the source section’s ص ل ي root.
The fate of the people of the left includes burning in Hell; the word for that burning belongs to the ص ل ي root that the source section also links to prayer.
The command to burn the condemned in Hell uses the same ص ل ي root as the source section’s fire-entry word.
The threat to burn a denier in Saqar uses the exact ص ل ي root that the source section also hears in prayer.
After being veiled from their Lord, these deniers are said to burn in Hell; this is another direct use of the source section’s ص ل ي fire-entry root.
The condemned will burn in a blazing fire; the ayah uses the source section’s ص ل ي root in the same fire-entry sense.
Abu Lahab is promised burning in a flaming fire, another direct instance of the source section’s ص ل ي fire-entry root.
The concluding image is a حَامِيَة fire, the same distinctive hot-fire description as 88:4, now attached to the fate of one whose scale is light.

This says all in heaven and earth prostrate to God willingly or unwillingly; its explicit willing/compelled boundary sharpens the source section’s contrast between worldly invitation and judgment-day inability.
David falls bowing and turns back after recognizing his trial; the source section says a bowed face also evokes the raki, making this chosen bowing a counterpart to humiliation.
When the Qur’an is recited, people given knowledge fall in prostration; this is the voluntary response whose judgment-day counterpart the source section finds in 68:43.
When reminded of God’s signs, believers fall in prostration, glorify Him, and are not arrogant; this joins reminder to voluntary sujud, against the later forced call.
When the Qur’an is recited, these people do not prostrate; their refusal is a specific worldly counterpart to the later call to sujud described in 68:43.
This description of repentant worshippers names them as bowing and prostrating, the ritual bodily acts the source section hears beside its words for bowed faces and burning.
The battle prayer is arranged around one group prostrating while the other keeps watch, then the second group praying; it gives a concrete scene of prayer’s bodily sujud under strain.
At the close of a warning, the audience is commanded to prostrate and worship; it is a direct voluntary call that contrasts with the later inability in 68:43.
These believers remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides, then pray to be protected from the Fire; the ayah joins bodily states, remembrance, supplication, and fire in one scene.
When God is mentioned, hearts tremble; the same ayah names patience through affliction and maintaining prayer, connecting remembrance and bodily endurance to worship.
The revealed word makes skins shiver, then soften at God’s remembrance; this gives a bodily response to dhikr alongside the source section’s connection between bodily submission and remembrance.
The night command explicitly requires standing for prayer except for a little; 73:20 later explains the long vigil’s burden and relief, giving context for the source section’s weary upright stance.
The preceding 94:7 commands exertion; this ayah directs the longing toward the Lord, completing the devotional orientation of the standing-and-effort command quoted by the source section.
Some People of the Book are described as خَاشِعِينَ لله while believing in revelation; the source section’s root for a bowed face thus also marks voluntary humility before God.
This commands calling on God humbly and privately; it concretely connects the source section’s dictionary sense of dhikr as supplication with voluntary humility rather than judgment-day disgrace.
God invites people to call on Him, while those too proud to worship will enter Hell humbled; this directly joins supplication, refusal of worship, punishment, and humiliation.

On the Day of Resurrection, faces are humbled before the Living and wrongdoing is disappointed; this is a judgment-day face posture distinct from the source section’s bowed face, but concretely echoes its scene.
The disbelievers are thrust toward the Fire of Hell; this forced movement toward burning contrasts with the call to prostrate in 68:43 and extends the source section’s judgment scene.
The passage names the blazing fire Laza, another direct fire scene for the source section’s image of entering a hot fire.
This ayah describes the flame stripping the scalp; 70:15 names Laza, while this ayah adds the burning body’s injury to the source section’s fire image.
The preceding ayat establish Laza as a destructive flame; this ayah says it calls whoever turned away, joining the fire to the same turning-away stance named in the source section.
